summary: Defines context replication for Robust Header Compression, a complement to context initialization in RFC 3095. A new compression context can be created based on an existing one, reducing the overhead of setting up short-lived flows. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: If a new sheet of notes starts like an old one, you can copy it and change a few lines. This memo lets compression start by copying settings from an earlier conversation.

questions: what is a base context in rohc
when does rohc use a static nack
subtitle: Lets a header compressor start a new flow by copying most of its settings from a flow that already works.

tldr.problem: Every new flow normally has to send most of its header information uncompressed before small compressed headers can be used. Many short-lived flows between the same two ends waste much of the gain from header compression.
tldr.mechanism: Context replication creates a new context from an already validated base context. The compressor sends a special IR-CR packet that points to the base context and carries only the fields that differ.
tldr.outcome: Profiles that choose to support it can get some compression from the very first packet of a flow. The catch is that corruption of one context can now spread to another.

today: RFC 4164 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3095.

sections.title: Why Replicate a Context
sections.content:
Flows that pass through the same compressor and decompressor often share header fields. Some of what a new flow needs to establish is therefore already present at the decompressor. Context replication reuses that information, and it is especially useful when many short-lived flows, such as short TCP transfers, run at the same time or nearly so.

With replication, fields such as the IP source or destination address (16 octets each for IPv6) can be left out of the special packet, and ports can be omitted or sent in compressed form from the first packet. The mechanism is general and any ROHC profile may define support for it. It builds on the framework in RFC 3095.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you keep filling in the same form for every visit. If most of the form is the same as last time, you only write down what changed.

sections.title: Base Contexts and Control Fields
sections.content:
A base context is a context that both the compressor and the decompressor have validated. The Base CID (BCID) is the context identifier of that base context. Replication copies information from it into a new context.

Only the decompressor is required to support replication in profiles that define it. Using the IR-CR packet is optional for the compressor. Profiles SHOULD say, for each control field (such as the NBO and RND flags or the mode of operation), whether its value is copied from the base context or reinitialized. A compressor MUST NOT start replication while a control field that is not reinitialized is being updated, for example during a mode transition handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: The base context is the old sheet of notes both sides already agree on. Some notes get copied over, and some start fresh.

sections.title: The Compressor and the CR State
sections.content:
ROHC compression normally starts in the IR state, where packets carry all fields in full. Replication adds a CR state in which the compressor sends a mix of compressed and uncompressed data plus a reference to a base context. The compressor can move from IR to CR when it can select a suitable base context. This is optional and does not change the existing transitions.

The base context MUST have been acknowledged by the decompressor using the CRC option in feedback, its static part MUST have been acknowledged, and it MUST be valid at replication time. Replication therefore needs a feedback channel. Even then, only a high degree of confidence is possible, because the base context could be damaged or discarded after it was acknowledged. What counts as a suitable base context is left to implementations.

From CR the compressor moves to a higher compression state by the optimistic approach (for instance after sending several IR-CR packets with the same information) or on an ACK. On a STATIC-NACK it MUST fall back to its initial no-context state and SHOULD re-initialize the decompressor with an IR packet. A NACK means the static part is probably still valid but the dynamic part is not.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender tries a shortcut only if it knows the receiver already has a good old sheet. If the receiver says it did not work, the sender goes back to writing everything out.

sections.title: The Decompressor Side
sections.content:
On receiving an IR-CR packet, the decompressor uses the profile field to decide how to process it. If the 8-bit CRC fails, the packet MUST be discarded. If the profile uses a Base CID and the field is present, that identifies the base context; otherwise the packet's own CID is used.

The decompressor builds the new context from the packet plus the base context and rebuilds the header. The 7-bit CRC over the original uncompressed header MUST be used to verify the result. On success it initializes or updates the context and SHOULD send an ACK. If the check fails, the context MUST NOT be changed.

If validation fails on the first IR-CR packets, the decompressor MUST invalidate the context and SHOULD send a STATIC-NACK. A decompressor that deletes state when a flow ends SHOULD do this too, so the compressor does not keep a stale CID as a base. If the context was valid and later packets fail, it SHOULD send a NACK. Feedback for an IR or IR-CR packet SHOULD use the CRC option.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the shortcut message twice. If the check numbers do not match, it ignores the message and says so.

sections.title: The IR-CR Packet
sections.content:
The IR-CR packet is an IR packet with the one spare profile-specific bit (x) used as a flag, though profiles may identify IR-CR another way. After the type octet come the CID, a 1-octet Profile (the 8 least significant bits of the profile identifier), a 1-octet CRC, profile-specific information and the payload. The profile-specific part is defined by each profile and MUST include a 7-bit CRC over the original uncompressed header. Which fields are replicated is outside this document.

The two CRCs differ. The 8-bit CRC covers the whole packet except the payload, including the CID or Add-CID octet and the Base CID field. Its polynomial is C(x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^8. The 7-bit CRC covers the original header and uses C(x) = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + x^6 + x^7. Both start with the register preset to all 1's.

The Base CID may differ from the new flow's CID. If they are equal, the base context is overwritten. With small CIDs the BCID is a four-bit field (0 to 15). With large CIDs it takes one or two octets, coded like a large CID. The IR-CR is not recommended for repairing a damaged context.
sections.plainLanguage: The shortcut message has a label saying which rulebook to use, a pointer to the old sheet, and two check numbers so the receiver can tell if it got scrambled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not believe replication adds new weaknesses beyond those listed in RFC 3095. It does increase the impact of those attacks by creating dependencies between contexts. Corruption of one context can make the compressor's attempts to initialize another context fail, or can carry over to another context if a corrupted context is used as the base.
sections.plainLanguage: If you copy from a smudged sheet, the smudge gets copied too. So one bad sheet can now spoil others.

sections.title: Replication Across Profiles
sections.content:
An informative appendix looks at replicating between different profiles. This is not supported as defined. A profile's context entries can differ in content, representation and structure, because profiles may use different encoding methods for the same field. A compressor therefore cannot use a base context from another profile unless that profile explicitly provides the mapping, or both are defined formally with ROHC-FN in a compatible way.

Existing decompressors of other profiles would need to be updated, so the RFC says this cannot be treated as an implementation-specific issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying notes only works if both notebooks are written in the same style. Different styles need a translation guide first.

viz.caption: FIXED OCTETS OF THE IR-CR PACKET (CID, profile-specific part and payload omitted)

fields.name: IR type octet
fields.desc: Bit pattern 1111110x; x is the profile-specific bit.

fields.name: Profile
fields.desc: The 8 least significant bits of the profile identifier.

fields.name: CRC
fields.desc: 8-bit CRC over the packet except the payload.
